title: The first crib (Greccio, 1223)
hook: Francis sets up a manger with an ox and donkey so people can see

segments.voice: Yesterday, San Damiano, and a cross that asked Francis to repair a house. Your line was start with stones.

A bundle of hay. An ox. A donkey. A rough wooden feeding trough in a hillside village called Greccio, in the middle of a winter night. People climb up from the farms with candles and torches, and the woods fill with light and singing. In Celano's telling no one lays a baby in the straw. There's a manger, two animals breathing in the cold, and a small man in a patched habit, overflowing with joy. Francis of Assisi has asked a friend to build this.
screen: `HAY, AN OX, A DONKEY.` → `TORCHES ON A WINTER NIGHT.` → `AN EMPTY MANGER.`

segments.voice: Thomas of Celano, who wrote an early life of Francis, says Francis wanted to see with his own eyes how the child of Bethlehem had lain in a manger, the hardship of it, the ox and the ass standing by. He had heard the Christmas story all his life. He wanted the village to see it, not only hear it. The Gospel line he had in mind is Luke's, which in the Douay-Rheims reads: "and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." The animals aren't in Luke. They come from the prophet Isaiah: "The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib." A beast, the prophet says, knows where its food comes from. Tradition placed those two beside the manger, and Francis put real ones there. A priest celebrated Mass right over the manger. Francis, who was a deacon and never a priest, sang the Gospel and preached, and Celano says he called Jesus the child of Bethlehem, saying the word Bethlehem so tenderly it sounded like a lamb's bleat. Celano adds that one man there saw a child lying in the manger as if asleep, and Francis seemed to wake him. Celano doesn't call Greccio the first of anything; first is the title tradition gave it later. What Greccio gave was a habit. Catholic homes and parishes still set out a crib in Advent, with an ox and a donkey nearby. A faith you can stand in front of, and see.
screen: `HE WANTED TO SEE IT WITH HIS EYES.` · `THE OX AND ASS COME FROM ISAIAH.` · `MASS SUNG OVER THE MANGER.` · `A HABIT THAT STAYED.` · then, large: `NO ROOM FOR THEM IN THE INN.`

segments.voice: Choose one small thing that keeps your faith, or whatever you hold dear, in sight: a crucifix moved to where you'll pass it, a holy card, a candle, a photo of someone you pray for or simply love. Picture it in its place and look at it the way the people at Greccio looked at the manger. If you pray, let the sight of it be the prayer.
Greccio. The hillside village where Francis set out a manger with an ox and a donkey so people could see the Christmas story. Today's word.
Your line: so they could see. Some things are better shown than told. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic families and parishes set up a crib, or nativity scene, for Advent and Christmas; some wait until Christmas Eve to lay the figure of the child in the manger.

chat.says: Who decided to put an ox and a donkey in the manger scene?
options: They come from Isaiah; tradition set them by the manger, and Francis used real ones.
Luke's Gospel names them, standing beside the manger where the baby lay.
The shepherds brought them along when they came to see the baby that night.
chat.meaning: Luke mentions only the manger. The ox and ass come from Isaiah; tradition put them beside it, and Francis set real ones there at Greccio.

notes: Year 1223 appears only in the index title; not spoken.
Index word 'The first crib' kept exactly; the teach says 'first' is tradition's title and that earlier Christmas images and plays existed. Confirm phrasing.

Celano details paraphrased: Francis wanting to see the infant's hardship with bodily eyes; torches and candles; Mass over the manger; Francis as deacon singing the Gospel; 'Bethlehem' spoken like a lamb's bleat; the vision of the child seeming to wake. Confirm each against Celano I, 84–86.
'In the oldest telling, no baby doll': Celano describes an empty manger with a vision of a child; confirm.
Isaiah 1:3 Douay-Rheims wording and 'tradition placed those two animals beside the manger': confirm.
Original: Vulgate Luke 2:7 'in praesepio'; nominative praesepe/praesepium. Confirm form and pronunciation.

Second editor pass: cut the unsourced 'nobody in the crowd is acting'; 'can hardly speak for joy' (which clashed with Francis singing the Gospel and preaching) changed to 'overflowing with joy', closer to Celano.
